chunks: A number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ibn Mahbub, from Hafs ibn Ghiyath, from Hajjaj, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him), who said:
The body becomes insolent when it does not fall ill, and there is no goodness in a body that does not experience illness to humble it.

key_terms.أَشِرَ: to become insolent, arrogant, or unruly — referring to the state of pride and excess that arises from unchecked ease and comfort
key_terms.الْجَسَدُ: the body (jasad) — referring to the physical human form, which in Islamic tradition is a trust from God requiring care and humility
key_terms.بِأَشَرٍ: by a measure of insolence/excess — indicating that a moderate experience of illness is a corrective grace

ai.seo_question: What did Imam al-Baqir say about the spiritual benefit of illness and sickness?
ai.summary: Imam Muhammad al-Baqir (peace be upon him) teaches that illness serves a spiritually purifying function: a body that never experiences sickness becomes arrogant and unruly. This hadith reframes physical illness not as a misfortune but as a divine mercy that prevents the soul and body from succumbing to pride and excess. In the early Islamic context, where physical hardship was a common reality, this teaching would have provided profound comfort and a theological framework for understanding suffering.
